- Card, fact: The card says Jefferson drafted the Declaration in July 1776, after Congress had chosen to break away. He drafted it in June 1776, after the committee was appointed on 11 June. Congress voted for independence on 2 July and adopted the Declaration on 4 July, so the draft came before the vote, not after it.

The intended answer, Paine, still stands because Common Sense came out in January 1776.

rejected.title: Individuals on the road to independence
card: George III
King of Britain from 1760. He opposed the American cause and backed Parliament's right to tax the colonies, so the Declaration of Independence blamed him for the colonists' grievances.
Samuel Adams and John Hancock
Adams was a Boston organiser who led protests against British rule from the 1760s. Hancock was a wealthy Boston merchant who funded the cause and became president of the Continental Congress in 1775.
Thomas Paine and Thomas Jefferson

Paine's pamphlet Common Sense, published in January 1776, attacked monarchy itself and sold widely, turning many colonists toward independence. Jefferson drafted the Declaration of Independence in July 1776, after Congress had chosen to break away.
George Washington
A Virginian chosen by the Continental Congress in 1775 to command the Continental Army against British forces.
rejected.remember: Each figure shaped independence differently: by resisting it, organising, funding, persuading, drafting or commanding.

a.q: Which figure shaped the road to independence while opposing it?
a.why: George III backed Parliament's right to tax the colonies, and the Declaration blamed him for their grievances, so his role pushed colonists toward a break. Hancock is tempting as a wealthy, established figure, but he funded the cause and led the Continental Congress.
a.clue: Think about who the colonists blamed.

b.q: A historian argues one figure did most to win public opinion over to independence in early 1776. Which figure best fits this argument?
opts: Samuel Adams, through protests in Boston
George Washington, through his army command
b.why: Common Sense came out in January 1776, attacked monarchy and sold widely, so it shifted many colonists toward independence. Jefferson is tempting, but he drafted the Declaration in July, after Congress had already chosen to break away, so it announced a decision rather than winning people over to it.
b.clue: Check which writing came before Congress made its choice.

draft.title: Leaders of the American cause
card: George III
King of Britain from 1760. He backed Parliament's right to tax and govern the colonies, and the Declaration of Independence blamed him for the colonists' grievances.
Samuel Adams and John Hancock
Adams was a Massachusetts organiser who stirred up opposition to British rule. Hancock was a wealthy Boston merchant who used his money and standing to support the cause.
Thomas Paine and Thomas Jefferson
Paine wrote Common Sense in 1776, a pamphlet that urged independence in plain language. Jefferson was the main author of the Declaration of Independence.
George Washington
A Virginian who was chosen by the Continental Congress to command the Continental Army in 1775.
draft.remember: Each leader shaped independence in a different way: ruling, organising, funding, writing or commanding.

a.q: Which leader is best described as the main author of the Declaration of Independence?
a.why: Jefferson drafted the Declaration. Paine is the tempting choice because he also wrote for independence, but his work was the pamphlet Common Sense, not the Declaration.
a.clue: Think of who wrote the document, not the pamphlet.

b.q: In 1776, a printer in Philadelphia wants to hand out a short, plain-language text to persuade ordinary colonists to back independence. Which leader's work should he print?
opts: George III's defence of Parliament's right to tax
George Washington's orders to the Continental Army
John Hancock's accounts as a Boston merchant
b.why: Paine wrote Common Sense in plain language to win ordinary colonists over to independence. Washington's orders were about commanding the army, and George III opposed independence, so neither would persuade colonists to support it.
b.clue: Which leader wrote a pamphlet aimed at ordinary people?

problems.detail: The title 'Leaders of the American cause' covers George III, who opposed the American cause. Students could come away thinking he was one of its leaders.

The question's wording ('short, plain-language text to persuade ordinary colonists') repeats the card's description of Common Sense almost word for word. The distractors are implausible: army orders, the king's defence of taxation and merchant accounts. This is too easy for Year 12.
The clue 'not the pamphlet' rules out Paine, the only tempting distractor, which leaves Jefferson as an obvious pick. The question also repeats the card's exact phrase 'main author'.
